You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

Computing totals: full defection yields each person 2 net points from their tokens plus base, while full cooperation yields 6 points each—so cooperation is socially superior even though keeping tokens is the individually dominant strategy. Since this is a repeated 10-round game rather than one-shot, I'm weighing whether early cooperation could help establish trust and sustain higher joint payoffs despite the individual incentive to defect.

If everyone cooperates fully, each ends up with 24 points, better than the 20 each gets from mutual defection — so cooperation is collectively optimal even though defecting individually nets 14 more points, since the externality cost of keeping tokens is spread across the group rather than borne by me alone.

Given it's a 10-round game, I think a reasonable opening move is to signal cooperation by contributing the full 20 to the group and see how others respond.
